title: “Girls Chance Music” is running though June 21st at Vineyard Theatre ...
transcript: This coming of age story set in a girls summer music program, assembles an impressive ensemble of actor musicians, and it definitely struck a chord with me. Girls Chance Music is written by Eisa Davis, who some of you might know as the co-writer of the upcoming Warriors musical with Lin-Manuel Miranda. But of course, she's a very accomplished playwright in her own right. This one has kind of a tender, meditative quality. Sometimes we sit for long stretches and watch their music performances, or class exercises. It felt a little bit like Stereophonic meets Initiative, which, funny enough, both of those were very long plays, and I actually wondered if this one might have benefited from a similar treatment: making full use of the kind of slow burn vibe that the play already has to take us on a longer, more fleshed out journey with these teenagers. cause as it stands, sometimes the tone felt a little bit at odds with the drama, which kind of muddied the storytelling a little bit. Even with that unevenness, I was still very much on board for this. I really liked both of the lead characters and I found myself rooting for them. And some of that is how they're written on the page, But I also found the performances from Hillary Fisher and Naomi Latta particularly captivating all of which really went a long way to keeping me on the plays hook. And I found myself really moved by the themes. It's essentially this coming of age story, but with music as a thematic backdrop, kind of paralleling the things that you learn in arts education and carry with you into adulthood with the fleeting but powerful bonds that you make with your peers at that formative age. I'll admit there was also some personal nostalgia for me here, which like in many ways my experience is not at all like these characters, but much LIKE these characters. I also spent multiple summers in Berkeley, California, as a teenager in an arts program. And even some of the reflection that the protagonist has at the very end of the play mirrors some reflections I've had in my own life. So maybe I'm a little biased. And maybe that encouraged me to overlook some of the sections of the play that didn't work as well. But I also think my response to it is kind of a testament to the emotionally resonant bedrock of the story.
